# Background
Literature published in peer-reviewed papers specifically estimating the local economic impacts of data centers is extremely limited. Consequently, we expanded our scope to include preprint sources, such as those published on the Social Science Research Network (SSRN), and personal publications by academics. This expanded search yielded two key papers: The Local Economic Effects of Data Center Entry by Daniel Yue and Yiyang Zeng, and Data Centers and Local Job Creation by Michael J. Hicks.

Dr. Yue and Dr. Zeng use data center data sourced from Aterio and run difference-in-differences analyses, splitting their data into rural and metropolitan-classified counties. They test the impact of a county receiving its first data center on employment, wages, business establishment count, median household income, unemployment rates, building permits, and electricity prices. Five years after a county receives a data center, the authors find statistically significant increases in employment (+3.5%), wages (+5.0%), business establishments (+4.7%), median household income (+1.9%), and housing construction permits (+16%). The effect on unemployment was statistically insignificant, and the impacts on electricity prices were difficult to interpret. The effects on employment, wages, and business establishments were found to be significant in metro counties but not in rural ones. Conversely, non-metro counties showed a significant decline in unemployment rates that was not present in metro counties. 

Dr. Hicks’s paper looks only at data centers in Texas and does not make a distinction between rural and urban counties. Like Dr. Yue and Dr. Zeng, he leverages difference-in-differences models to test the impact of data center entry into a county on local economic variables. Hicks’s analysis window covers only eight quarters, or two years, before and after the event, which could hide impacts that take longer to materialize. Overall, this paper does not find substantial impacts on labor markets, with the potential exception of very large-scale AI data centers. It does find a short-term boost in construction immediately after a data center enters a county, which quickly fades.

In addition to the standard economic outcomes analyzed by Dr. Yue, Dr. Zeng, and Dr. Hicks, we researched potential environmental variables that we could incorporate directly into an economic framework. Due to data availability limitations, we ended up narrowing our scope to include only air quality. The Cloud Next Door: Investigating the Environmental and Socioeconomic Strain of Datacenters on Local Communities by Ngata et al. highlights that nitrogen oxides (NOx​) and fine particulate matter (PM2.5​) are the primary air pollutants associated with data centers and proposes that a mix of on-site diesel backup power generators and induced power demand on fossil-fuel power plants are the main mechanisms by which data centers cause air pollution. Health-Informed Computing: Estimating and Addressing the Public Health Impact of Data Centers by Han et al. also links data centers to increases in NOx​ and PM2.5​ air pollution, as well as sulfur dioxide (SO2​), and estimates the economic costs associated with negative health outcomes. Estimating the Health and Economic Impacts of Changes in Local Air Quality by Carvour et al. goes further by estimating the dollar value associated with lower work productivity caused by marginal changes in air pollution.

## Data Sourcing & Organization
We have seven primary data sources: the CDC for air quality, the USDA for unemployment, the National Cancer Institute for population, Data.gov for construction permits, the BEA for GDP and personal income, the BLS for data centers, and the Census Bureau for business statistics. Augmenting our primary sources, we have three supporting sources: the Census Bureau for county sizes, NAICS code definitions, and FIPS codes; California Health and Human Services for county centroids; and Plotly Sample Datasets for mapping county borders. (Additional information and links for all sources can be found in Table A.1 of the Appendix.)

All primary sources were selected because they met both our time criteria of covering at least 2007 to 2022 and our granularity criteria of including data at the county level for all states in the contiguous U.S. All primary datasets already use the Federal Information Processing Standard (FIPS) code system to uniquely identify counties, naturally making a combination of year and county FIPS code the primary composite key for most of our database tables. For datasets that include NAICS codes, the primary key is a composite of NAICS code, year, and county code.

## Database Design
We chose a PostgreSQL database for this project. To avoid unnecessary costs and complexity, we decided against hosting it on a cloud service. Instead, we wrote a database creation script in Python and committed it to our repository. This allowed each team member to recreate the database locally, and whenever updates were pushed, everyone could simply rerun the local script to sync their local environment.

The database is designed to comply with Third Normal Form (3NF), which balances data integrity and ease of access. Every table contains a primary key, implemented as a composite key using combinations of year, county ID, and NAICS code, depending on the table. 

Our primary tables are stored in the public schema, which is depicted in Figure 1. After initializing our primary tables, we create copies within a separate schema called “transformed” inside the database. In this schema, we calculate and store spatial calculation versions for all relevant columns. We calculate spatial effects for most features by using inverse-distance-weighted averages or sums across the five nearest counties in our cluster-based analysis. To find nearby data centers, we draw a 50-mile buffer around each county and estimate data center presence outside the target county by multiplying the total number of data centers in each nearby county by the percentage of the county that overlaps the buffer and summing those estimates. Maintaining separate schemas allows us to maintain idempotency so that we can alter the primary tables as needed without causing dependency issues in our transformed tables.

## Data Cleaning
Although our data is stored in a PostgreSQL database, we executed all data cleaning in Python to maintain consistency with our downstream modeling pipeline. We created an individual Python cleaning script for each distinct data source. Each script imports raw CSV files and applies a standardized sequence of cleaning operations, including checking for missing values, correcting data types, standardizing formats, and removing duplicate rows. Once basic cleaning is complete, the script handles any necessary data conversions or transformations. Finally, the script uses SQLAlchemy to ingest and write the cleaned data directly into its designated table in the database.

Once the initial cleaning pass completes in Python and the tables are populated in PostgreSQL, we run a series of SQL data quality checks. These queries verify that every row across all tables uniquely joins to the central U.S. counties table, ensure there are no duplicate rows, and confirm that each table contains the same number of counties as our primary reference list. If a data table contains unmatched or unexpected counties, our checks flag them immediately. We then trace these issues back to the specific Python cleaning script for that data source, apply the necessary corrections, re-ingest the data, and rerun the SQL verification queries in an iterative loop until no mismatches remain.

Our SQL data quality queries uncovered persistent inconsistencies in county FIPS codes across our analysis window, particularly due to boundary changes, splits, and reclassifications in Virginia and Connecticut. Virginia contains independent cities that lie entirely within a surrounding parent county. When a data source reported separate statistics for an independent city and its parent county, we aggregated those figures and assigned the combined total to the parent county. This standardized our data to match the coarser granularity used by sources that already pre-aggregate those regions. For isolated independent cities located outside Virginia, we used a similar methodology, identifying the primary surrounding county and attributing the independent city's data directly to that surrounding county.
In 2022, Connecticut officially retired its historical county system in favor of new planning regions with completely redrawn geographic boundaries. Because the 2022 boundaries no longer aligned with historical data, we dropped the reported 2022 values for Connecticut and handled that final year using imputation.

## Managing Missingness
Because a historical dataset tracking precise data center locations and construction dates was unavailable, we utilized the Bureau of Labor Statistics' Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW). This quarterly report spans our full analysis window and details establishment counts by NAICS industry codes. We focused on code 518 (Data Processing, Hosting, and Related Services), which aligns closely with the operational definition of a data center. We used this code to construct a database table tracking annual 518 establishment counts per county.
While all of our data sources had data from 2001 through 2022, we had to restrict our timeline to start in 2007. That was the last major revision year for the NAICS 518 classification, making it the farthest we could go back and still be confident that the code identified the same type of establishment from one year to the next.

Within our limited time frame, we found that certain counties exhibited sporadic missing records where 518 establishments existed prior to and following an intervening gap. Because the QCEW explicitly records true zero values (0) for counties without qualifying establishments, we treated these omitted intermediate records as data collection/reporting gaps rather than closures.
To resolve these missing intermediate years, we applied linear interpolation across the gap between the last known active year and the subsequent reporting year. We also created a flag in our data center table to track which values were imputed. If a county was missing values for some but not all years, and that missingness occurred at either the start or end of our time frame, we assumed those values were zero for our linear imputation. 

A similar pattern of data holes appeared in our air quality data. Starting in 2020 and extending through the end of our analysis window, we observed that a small subset of counties previously present in the air quality dataset began reporting missing values. To address this, we implemented a spatial fill function based on inverse distance weighting. For any missing county in a given year, the function calculates a weighted average of air quality using its five nearest neighboring counties, measuring distance from the centroid of the missing county to the centroids of its neighbors. We used this weighted average to impute the missing county values for 2020 and repeated the process for the remaining missing years.
